sciXsBallStk: A ball-and-stick model has 1 H ball + 1 Cl ball joined by sticks. Which formula does it show?
One hydrogen atom bonded to one chlorine atom is hydrogen chloride, HCl.
A ball-and-stick model has 1 C ball + 1 O ball joined by sticks. Which formula does it show?
One carbon atom and one oxygen atom make carbon monoxide, CO.
A ball-and-stick model has 1 N ball + 2 O balls joined by sticks. Which formula does it show?
One nitrogen and two oxygen atoms give the formula NO₂.
A ball-and-stick model has 2 N balls + 1 O ball joined by sticks. Which formula does it show?
Two nitrogen atoms and one oxygen atom give the formula N₂O.
A ball-and-stick model has 1 S ball + 2 O balls joined by sticks. Which formula does it show?
One sulfur atom with two oxygen atoms is sulfur dioxide, SO₂.
A ball-and-stick model has 1 S ball + 3 O balls joined by sticks. Which formula does it show?
One sulfur atom with three oxygen atoms is sulfur trioxide, SO₃.
A ball-and-stick model has 2 H balls + 1 S ball joined by sticks. Which formula does it show?
Two hydrogen atoms bonded to one sulfur atom give H₂S.
A ball-and-stick model has 2 Cl balls joined by sticks. Which formula does it show?
Two chlorine atoms joined together form a chlorine molecule, Cl₂.
A ball-and-stick model has 3 O balls joined by sticks. Which formula does it show?
Three oxygen atoms bonded in one molecule make ozone, O₃.
A ball-and-stick model has 1 C ball + 4 Cl balls joined by sticks. Which formula does it show?
One carbon atom bonded to four chlorine atoms gives CCl₄.
A ball-and-stick model has 2 C balls + 6 H balls joined by sticks. Which formula does it show?
Two carbon atoms and six hydrogen atoms make ethane, C₂H₆.
A ball-and-stick model has 3 C balls + 8 H balls joined by sticks. Which formula does it show?
Three carbon atoms and eight hydrogen atoms make propane, C₃H₈.
A ball-and-stick model has 2 C balls + 4 H balls joined by sticks. Which formula does it show?
Two carbon atoms and four hydrogen atoms give ethene, C₂H₄.
A ball-and-stick model has 1 H ball + 1 F ball joined by sticks. Which formula does it show?
One hydrogen atom bonded to one fluorine atom is hydrogen fluoride, HF.
A ball-and-stick model has 1 C ball + 2 S balls joined by sticks. Which formula does it show?
One carbon atom with two sulfur atoms gives carbon disulfide, CS₂.
A ball-and-stick model has 1 P ball + 3 H balls joined by sticks. Which formula does it show?
One phosphorus atom bonded to three hydrogen atoms gives PH₃.
A ball-and-stick model has 2 H balls joined by sticks. Which formula does it show?
Two hydrogen atoms bonded together form one hydrogen molecule, H₂.
A ball-and-stick model has 1 C ball + 2 H balls + 1 O ball joined by sticks. Which formula does it show?
One carbon, two hydrogen and one oxygen atom give the formula CH₂O.
Which ball-and-stick model matches the formula CH₄?
1 C ball joined to 4 H balls
4 C balls joined to 1 H ball
1 C ball joined to 2 H balls
2 C balls joined to 4 H balls
The subscript 4 belongs to H, so the model needs one carbon ball and four hydrogen balls.
Which ball-and-stick model matches the formula SO₂?
1 S ball joined to 2 O balls
2 S balls joined to 1 O ball
1 S ball joined to 3 O balls
2 S balls joined to 2 O balls
SO₂ has no subscript on S (meaning 1) and a subscript 2 on O.
Which ball-and-stick model matches the formula C₂H₆O?
2 C, 6 H and 1 O balls joined
6 C, 2 H and 1 O balls joined
2 C, 6 H and 2 O balls joined
1 C, 6 H and 2 O balls joined
The subscripts show 2 carbon, 6 hydrogen and 1 oxygen atom.
How many balls in total are in a ball-and-stick model of CO₂?
CO₂ has one carbon atom and two oxygen atoms, so the model has 3 balls.
sciXsElCmpM: What does this model show? Many separate grey balls that are all the same and not joined (helium)
Every particle is the same single kind of atom, so it is an element.
What does this model show? Many pairs of identical yellow-green balls joined (Cl₂)
Each molecule contains only chlorine atoms, so it is an element.
What does this model show? Every molecule is one black ball joined to four white balls (CH₄)
Each molecule has two different kinds of atoms bonded, so it is a compound.
What does this model show? Pairs of red balls (O₂) mixed with separate pairs of blue balls (N₂)
Two different elements are present but not bonded to each other, so it is a mixture of elements.
What does this model show? Water molecules (H₂O) mixed with carbon dioxide molecules (CO₂)
Two different compounds are present together without bonding, so it is a mixture of compounds.
What does this model show? Purple and green balls alternating in a repeating grid, all bonded (NaCl)
Sodium and chlorine are chemically combined in a fixed ratio, so it is a compound.
What does this model show? Every molecule is three identical red balls joined (O₃)
Ozone contains only oxygen atoms, so it is an element.
What does this model show? Single orange balls of one kind packed in neat rows (copper)
All the balls are the same kind of atom, so the model shows an element.
What does this model show? Every molecule is one white ball joined to one green ball (HCl)
Hydrogen and chlorine atoms are bonded together, which makes a compound.
What does this model show? Separate grey balls (helium) mixed with separate pink balls (neon), none joined
Two kinds of atoms are present but not bonded, so it is a mixture of elements.
What does this model show? Many pairs of identical white balls joined (H₂)
Each molecule contains only hydrogen atoms, so it is an element.
What does this model show? Every molecule is one black ball joined to one red ball (CO)
Carbon and oxygen are bonded together, so it is a compound.
What does this model show? CH₄ molecules mixed with NH₃ molecules
Two different compounds are mixed but not bonded to each other.
What does this model show? Every molecule is eight identical yellow balls joined in a ring (S₈)
The ring contains only sulfur atoms, so it is an element.
What does this model show? Every molecule is two black balls joined to six white balls (C₂H₆)
Carbon and hydrogen atoms are bonded in each molecule, so it is a compound.
What does this model show? Every molecule is one yellow ball joined to two red balls (SO₂)
Sulfur and oxygen atoms are bonded together in each identical molecule.
What does this model show? Pairs of white balls (H₂) mixed with pairs of red balls (O₂), not bonded to each other
Hydrogen and oxygen molecules are each elements, and here they are only mixed.
What does this model show? Layers of identical black balls all joined in sheets (graphite)
Graphite contains only carbon atoms, so it is an element.
What does this model show? Every molecule is one blue ball joined to two red balls (NO₂)
Nitrogen and oxygen atoms are bonded together, so it is a compound.
What does this model show? CO₂ molecules mixed with CO molecules
Both kinds of molecules are compounds, and they are mixed rather than bonded.
A model of N₂ shows two balls joined by a stick. Why is it an element?
Both balls are the same kind of atom
The balls are joined by a stick
It is a gas at room temperature
An element contains only one kind of atom, and both balls in N₂ are nitrogen.
In a model, every molecule has two different colours of balls joined together. What must the substance be?
Different kinds of atoms chemically joined in each molecule make a compound.
sciXsRxEnergy: Which describes the energy change? Natural gas burning in a furnace
Combustion gives off heat and light to the surroundings, so it is exothermic.
Which describes the energy change? Iron slowly rusting on a bike chain
Rusting slowly releases heat as iron combines with oxygen, so it is exothermic.
Which describes the energy change? Cells breaking down glucose in cellular respiration
Respiration releases energy stored in glucose, so it is exothermic.
Which describes the energy change? A candle burning on a table
Burning wax gives off heat and light, so energy is released.
Which describes the energy change? A glow stick giving off light after it is bent
The chemicals react and release energy as light, so the reaction is exothermic.
Which describes the energy change? An acid and a base mixing and the beaker getting warm
The beaker warms because the neutralization releases energy.
Which describes the energy change? Wet concrete warming up as it hardens
The setting reaction in concrete releases heat, so it is exothermic.
Which describes the energy change? Electricity splitting water into hydrogen and oxygen
Electrolysis needs a constant input of electrical energy, so it absorbs energy.
Which describes the energy change? Citric acid and baking soda in water making the cup feel cold
The cup cools because the reaction takes in thermal energy from its surroundings.
Which describes the energy change? Limestone breaking down into lime when heated in a kiln
The limestone only breaks down while heat is continually supplied, so it is endothermic.
Which describes the energy change? Cake batter turning into cake in a hot oven
Baking reactions happen only while the batter takes in heat from the oven.
Which describes the energy change? An egg white turning solid as it cooks in a pan
The egg changes only while it absorbs heat from the pan.
Which describes the energy change? Two powders mixed in a flask that freezes to a wet board underneath
Freezing the water under the flask shows the reaction absorbed lots of thermal energy.
Which describes the energy change? A thermite reaction producing molten iron and bright sparks
The thermite reaction gives off intense heat and light, so it is exothermic.
In an endothermic reaction, the temperature of the surroundings usually…
Energy is taken in from the surroundings, so they become cooler.
In an exothermic reaction, energy is…
Exothermic reactions give off energy, often as heat or light.
Energy must be put in to pull bonded atoms apart.
Energy is given off when atoms join to form bonds.
A reaction is exothermic overall when…
forming bonds releases more energy than breaking bonds absorbs
breaking bonds absorbs more energy than forming bonds releases
no bonds are broken and no bonds are formed
the atoms in the reactants are destroyed
If more energy comes out from new bonds than went into breaking old ones, the extra is released.
During a reaction, a thermometer rises from 20 °C to 35 °C. What does this show?
A temperature rise means the reaction released thermal energy into the mixture.
During a reaction, a thermometer drops from 22 °C to 9 °C. What does this show?
A temperature drop means the reaction took thermal energy from the mixture.
What happens to the total amount of energy during a chemical reaction?
It is conserved and only changes form
It is destroyed when bonds break
It is created when bonds form
Energy cannot be created or destroyed, so it is only transferred or transformed.
sciXsSoap: Besides soap, which product forms during saponification?
Glycerol
Ethanol
Carbon dioxide
Ammonia
When fats react with a strong base, they form soap and glycerol.
The long tail of a soap molecule is made mostly of…
carbon and hydrogen atoms
sodium and chlorine atoms
oxygen atoms only
iron and copper atoms
The tail is a hydrocarbon chain, a long chain of carbon and hydrogen atoms.
How is the tail of a soap molecule described?
Hydrophobic
Hydrophilic
Radioactive
Metallic
The hydrocarbon tail is water-fearing (hydrophobic) and mixes with oils instead.
In a micelle, which way do the soap molecules' tails point?
Inward, toward the trapped oil
Outward, toward the water
Upward, toward the air only
In completely random directions
The oil-loving tails gather around the oil in the centre while the heads face the water.
Why is soap called a surfactant?
It lowers the surface tension of water
It raises the surface tension of water
It floats only on the surface
It hardens any surface it touches
Surfactants lower surface tension, helping water spread and soak into dirt.
What type of substance is lye (sodium hydroxide)?
A strong base
A strong acid
A neutral salt
A pure element
Sodium hydroxide is a strong base, which is why it can react with fats to make soap.
Soap made with potassium hydroxide instead of sodium hydroxide tends to be…
softer, often a liquid soap
harder than sodium soap
a gas at room temperature
unable to clean at all
Potassium soaps are softer and are used for many liquid soaps.
Why is homemade cold-process soap left to cure for several weeks?
To let saponification finish and water evaporate
To let the bar grow larger over time
To change the soap into an acid
To let bacteria grow and clean it
Curing gives the reaction time to use up the lye and lets extra water leave, making a milder, harder bar.
Why is the pH of most bar soap above 7?
It is made using a base
It is made using an acid
It contains only pure water
It contains lots of vinegar
Soap is made from a strong base, so it is slightly basic.
Which of these can be used to make soap?
Olive oil, coconut oil or animal fat
Motor oil, gasoline or kerosene
Sugar, salt or baking soda
Sand, clay or chalk
Saponification needs fats or oils from plants or animals, which react with a strong base.
Fats and oils used in soapmaking are mostly molecules called…
triglycerides
proteins
nucleic acids
starches
Fats and oils are triglycerides, which the base splits into soap and glycerol.
How do synthetic detergents behave differently from soap in hard water?
They do not form scum with the minerals
They form more scum than soap does
They turn the hard water into ice
They only work in very salty water
Detergents are designed so hard-water minerals do not make them form scum.
Which dissolved minerals make water "hard"?
Calcium and magnesium
Sodium and potassium
Gold and silver
Helium and neon
Calcium and magnesium ions cause water hardness and react with soap to make scum.
Why does scrubbing your hands help soap work?
It helps soap surround and lift off oily dirt
It makes the soap molecules magnetic
It heats the water up to boiling
It changes the soap into an acid
Rubbing mixes soap with the oil so micelles can form and carry dirt away.
Why can water easily rinse away a micelle full of oil?
The heads on its outside attract water
The tails on its outside attract water
The trapped oil turns into water
Micelles are heavier than water
The water-loving heads face outward, so the whole micelle is carried by the water.
How can soap destroy some viruses, such as flu viruses?
It breaks apart their fatty outer layer
It freezes them solid
It turns them into bacteria
It gives them extra nutrients
Soap tails attach to the fatty envelope of these viruses and pull it apart.
Oil and water do not mix on their own. What does soap act as when it lets them mix?
An emulsifier
A catalyst
A fuel
A magnet
An emulsifier lets oil spread through water as tiny droplets.
What forms when tallow (beef fat) reacts with lye?
Soap and glycerol
Sugar and water
Salt and carbon dioxide
Oil and vinegar
Saponification of any fat with lye gives soap and glycerol.
Which observation shows that saponification has happened?
Oil and lye become a new solid substance
The oil simply floats on top
The lye completely evaporates
The mixture turns into pure water
A new substance with new properties forms, which shows a chemical reaction.
Which part of a soap molecule dissolves in grease?
The hydrocarbon tail
The charged head
The sodium ion
The water molecule
Like dissolves like, so the non-polar hydrocarbon tail mixes into non-polar grease.
When mixing a lye solution, why is lye added to water and not water to lye?
Water added to lye can boil and splash
Lye floats and will not mix otherwise
Water turns into lye if added second
Lye freezes if water is added to it
Adding water onto lye releases heat in a small spot, which can make the caustic mixture boil and spatter.
In bar soap, which ion is usually paired with the negatively charged head of each soap molecule?
Sodium ion, Na⁺
Chloride ion, Cl⁻
Oxide ion, O²⁻
Fluoride ion, F⁻
A negative head is attracted to a positive ion, and soap made with sodium hydroxide contains Na⁺.
sciXsFlavour: What is the Maillard reaction?
A reaction of sugars and amino acids that browns food
A reaction that makes food freeze faster
A reaction that removes all salt from food
A reaction between water and metals
When sugars and amino acids are heated together they form brown colours and new flavour compounds.
Caramelization happens when…
sugar is heated and breaks into new compounds
sugar is frozen into large crystals
salt dissolves in cold water
fat is mixed with vinegar
Heating sugar breaks it down into new molecules with caramel colour and flavour.
Esters, which give many fruits their smell, form when…
an acid reacts with an alcohol
a metal reacts with water
salt is mixed with sugar
two noble gases combine
An ester forms from the reaction of a carboxylic acid with an alcohol.
Which compound gives cinnamon its flavour?
Cinnamaldehyde
Capsaicin
Caffeine
Citric acid
Cinnamaldehyde is the main flavour molecule in cinnamon bark.
Which compound gives orange and lemon peels their scent?
Limonene
Vanillin
Menthol
Capsaicin
Limonene is the main aroma molecule in citrus peel oil.
Why does mint feel cool in your mouth?
Menthol activates cold-sensing receptors
Menthol lowers your mouth to 0 °C
Mint leaves contain tiny ice crystals
Menthol blocks all of your taste buds
Menthol triggers the same nerve receptors that sense cold, even though nothing gets colder.
Which basic taste is triggered by glutamate, found in tomatoes and parmesan?
Umami
Sour
Bitter
Salty
Glutamate fits umami receptors and gives a savoury taste.
Why does food taste bland when you have a stuffy nose?
Aroma molecules can't reach smell receptors
Your tongue stops making any saliva
Food molecules become much heavier
Your taste buds fall off your tongue
Much of flavour is smell, and a blocked nose stops aroma molecules reaching the receptors.
Two forms of carvone have the same atoms but are mirror images. Why does one smell like spearmint and the other like caraway?
Their shapes fit smell receptors differently
They have different numbers of atoms
One of them contains no carbon
One is a metal and one is a gas
Smell receptors respond to molecular shape, so mirror-image molecules can smell different.
Which ions give salty foods their salty taste?
Sodium ions
Iron ions
Hydrogen ions
Hydroxide ions
Salty taste mainly comes from sodium ions, such as those in table salt.
Sour taste is mostly caused by…
hydrogen ions from acids
sodium ions from salts
sugars from ripe fruit
fats from cooking oils
Acids release hydrogen ions, which sour taste receptors detect.
Coffee tastes bitter partly because it contains…
caffeine
sucrose
sodium chloride
vanillin
Caffeine is a bitter-tasting compound found in coffee and tea.
Why can a tiny amount of aspartame replace much more sugar?
It activates sweet receptors far more strongly
It is far heavier than table sugar
It is made of pure table salt
It blocks all of the other tastes
Aspartame's structure triggers sweet receptors about 200 times more strongly than sugar.
Why does crushing garlic make its smell much stronger?
Crushing starts a reaction that makes allicin
Crushing turns the garlic into salt
Crushing makes the garlic much colder
Crushing removes only the garlic's water
Breaking garlic cells lets an enzyme react with a compound to form strong-smelling allicin.
Why do ripe bananas taste sweeter than green bananas?
Starch breaks down into sugars as they ripen
Sugars turn into starch as they ripen
Ripe bananas absorb sugar from the air
The peel pumps salt into the fruit
Enzymes in ripening fruit break starch into sweet-tasting sugars.
Why does a cut apple turn brown and change flavour?
Enzymes help apple compounds react with oxygen
The apple soaks up brown light
The sugar in the apple melts
The apple's water turns into salt
Exposed apple compounds react with oxygen, helped by enzymes, forming brown products.
Why does drinking milk help after eating hot peppers?
Capsaicin dissolves in fat rather than water
Milk is colder than ice cubes
Milk is a strong acid that burns it off
Milk contains extra capsaicin
Capsaicin is fat-soluble, so the fat in milk helps wash it away from receptors.
Wintergreen flavour comes from methyl salicylate. Which group of compounds is it in?
Esters
Metals
Noble gases
Minerals
Methyl salicylate is an ester, like many other fruity and minty flavour molecules.
Why does warm food usually smell stronger than cold food?
More aroma molecules evaporate when it is warm
Warm food contains many more atoms
Cold food has no molecules at all
Cold food blocks your smell receptors
Heat gives molecules more energy, so more of them escape into the air and reach your nose.
How can chemists make an artificial pineapple flavour?
By making the same flavour molecule found in pineapple
By growing whole pineapples in test tubes
By adding yellow colouring to the food
By removing every molecule from the food
Flavour depends on the molecule, so making the same molecule (an ester) gives the same flavour.
How many basic tastes do human taste receptors detect?
Five
Two
Ten
Twenty
The five basic tastes are sweet, sour, salty, bitter and umami.
Why can a bitter taste act as a warning?
Many poisonous compounds taste bitter
Bitter foods are always too hot
All bitter foods contain salt
Bitter foods have no flavour molecules
Many harmful plant compounds are bitter, so disliking bitterness helps protect us.
